medical.title: Common airway bacterium may help prepare lungs to fight pneumonia
medical.summary: A common bacterium found in the mouth and airways may help the lungs better defend themselves against pneumonia, according to new research from the University of Colorado Anschutz.

medical.title: Protein LMOD1 offers new clues to muscle regeneration
medical.summary: Skeletal muscles are capable of regenerating themselves following an injury, a process that depends on muscle stem cells. In healthy resting muscle, these cells are predominantly in a quiescent state. However, following an injury, they are activated, begin to proliferate and subsequently start to develop into specialized skeletal muscle cells (differentiation). These cells then fuse with one another or with existing muscle fibers, generating new or repaired muscle fibers.

medical.title: Fruit fly study reveals how neural gates switch on short-term memory
medical.summary: A study in fruit flies led by researchers at NYU Langone Health has confirmed a long-standing suspicion about how the brain encodes short-term memories.

medical.title: Intranasal sufentanil-ketamine appears safe, effective for pediatric acute pain
medical.summary: Intranasal sufentanil-ketamine is fast-acting and appears to be well tolerated and effective at curbing acute pain for pediatric patients in the emergency department, according to a study presented at the annual European Emergency Medicine Congress, held Sept. 23–27 in Paris.

medical.title: Children living with sickle cell can be treated safely using hydroxyurea, 10-year trial finds
medical.summary: New research shows the efficacy and safety of hydroxyurea treatment for sickle cell anemia at four low-income sites in Africa, with no increase in clinically diagnosed infections.

medical.title: HPV vaccination before pregnancy linked to lower risk of preterm birth and other major complications
medical.summary: Receiving the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine before pregnancy is associated with a lower risk of major pregnancy complications, including preterm birth, with a greater reduction in risk seen among women vaccinated at an earlier age, according to a large Swedish study published by The BMJ.

medical.title: About 13% of newly qualified nurses and midwives leave hospital work within six years
medical.summary: The early years of working life differ for newly qualified nurses and midwives working in hospitals and comparable graduates working in other sectors. Louise Schubert Paaske, a Ph.D. student in health economics at the Danish Centre for Health Economics (DaCHE) at the University of Southern Denmark, and her colleagues have used Danish national registers to follow the graduates' health trajectories over their first six years in employment. The study is published in the journal Communications Health.

medical.title: Autonomous AI can increase clinical capacity for dermatologists
medical.summary: Autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) in urgent skin cancer pathways can increase clinical capacity for dermatologists, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology, held from Sept. 30 to Oct. 3 in Vienna.

medical.title: Blood flow directs signals that assign liver cells their jobs, mouse study finds
medical.summary: The liver is organized into distinct zones in which liver cells perform different functions. The blood vessels of the liver play an important role in this spatial organization: the endothelial cells lining the vessels provide signals that instruct neighboring liver cells and help determine their function. But how do endothelial cells know which signals to produce?

medical.title: Of mice and zebrafish: How scientists solved a decades-old mystery and uncovered new insights about inflammation
medical.summary: Sometimes you can solve a mystery with a fish but not a mouse. Sometimes you can see a biochemical process happening, but you can't study it in detail until you identify the underlying players. Sometimes separate streams of inquiry turn out to be part of the same story.

medical.title: Approved cancer drug may reduce kidney damage linked to nail-patella syndrome
medical.summary: Researchers led by Dr. Ralph Witzgall, a professor at the Chair of Molecular and Cellular Anatomy at the University of Regensburg, have deciphered a key disease mechanism underlying the hereditary kidney disorder nail-patella syndrome and identified a potential therapeutic strategy. Their findings demonstrate that an already approved drug can significantly reduce disease-causing changes. The study, which also involved researchers from the Technical University of Munich (TUM), was recently published in the journal Nature Communications.

medical.title: Blood marker may flag Alzheimer's-related changes in Down syndrome decades before symptoms appear
medical.summary: Decades before the first symptoms of Alzheimer's disease appear, some changes associated with the disease may begin to leave a trace in the blood. A study by the Sant Pau Research Institute (IR Sant Pau) has found that, in people with Down syndrome, levels of β-synuclein, a protein related to synaptic function, begin to rise in the third decade of life, long before symptoms appear and earlier than other blood biomarkers of Alzheimer's disease.

medical.title: Heart recovery technique adapted for pediatric transplants
medical.summary: A donor heart recovery technique developed at Vanderbilt Health has been successfully adapted for children by pediatric heart transplant surgeons at Monroe Carell Jr. Children's Hospital at Vanderbilt, potentially expanding access to lifesaving heart transplants for children.

medical.title: Flu season may be starting early; experts say get vaccinated now
medical.summary: Flu season may be getting a head start this year, and experts say that's a good reason not to put off your flu shot.

medical.title: Low-risk prostate tumors reveal molecular signs linked to more aggressive cancer
medical.summary: A new study revealed molecular features linked to more aggressive prostate cancer in a subset of patients who had been classified as low risk, highlighting biological differences that may not be apparent from clinical measures alone. The results could lead to new therapeutic strategies.

medical.title: First single-cell DNA analysis reveals mitochondrial damage in vulnerable Parkinson's brainstem neurons
medical.summary: Researchers have carried out the first single-cell analysis of mitochondrial DNA in a population of brainstem neurons that are particularly vulnerable to degeneration in Parkinson's disease.

science.title: How Spain's torrential rainstorms put sewage into its rivers and seas
science.summary: After heavy rain, Spanish cities often awaken to refreshed air and clean streets, while the rainwater itself vanishes into storm drains along with everything it swept away. Underground, however, a very different story unfolds.

science.title: Snowball Earth's iron deposits may have formed through microbes living without sunlight
science.summary: Iron is one of the most abundant metals on Earth's surface, yet how such massive iron ore deposits formed throughout geological history has long remained a mystery. The prevailing theory has been that ancient photosynthetic bacteria oxidized iron, causing it to precipitate and accumulate in the oceans.

science.title: From jargon to impact: Teaching undergraduates the art of public communication
science.summary: Articles published in The Conversation go well beyond academics writing for a general audience—they can also serve as valuable content for educators to use in the classroom.

science.title: Tiny photosynthetic organisms help transport carbon to the depths of the Baltic Sea
science.summary: Tiny photosynthetic organisms in the Baltic Sea can contribute substantially to the transport of carbon from surface waters to deeper parts of the sea. A new study from the Department of Ecology, Environment and Plant Sciences at Stockholm University shows that their ability to form colonies and aggregates is an important factor determining how much of their biomass sinks.

science.title: How a harmful bacterium senses iron—and why it matters for fighting infections
science.summary: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a common culprit in hospital-acquired bacterial infections and is growing more resistant to antibiotics. New findings from Aaron Smith, professor of chemistry and biochemistry at UMBC, and collaborators at Oklahoma State University show how a two-protein system inside the bacterium operates like a sensitive switch: The pair detects iron both outside and inside the cell and then rewrites large parts of the microbe's metabolism in response.

science.title: International experience gives business leaders an edge, study finds
science.summary: Business leaders with international experience play a significant role in shaping the success of their organizations and are often associated with stronger organizational performance, including higher growth, profitability and stock market performance, according to a new study published in the Journal of Management.

science.title: Superbug P. aeruginosa uses two protein plugs to seal channels against antibiotics
science.summary: A joint research team has identified a new mechanism underlying antibiotic resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a major multidrug-resistant "superbug." The discovery provides important clues for the development of new treatments for multidrug-resistant bacterial infections. The findings are published in the journal Nature Communications.

science.title: Chain reaction that begins when tumor suppression gene is switched off offers clues to how cancer develops
science.summary: A tumor suppressor gene known as p53 is mutated in more than half of all cancers, but how it acts to prevent cancer formation is largely unknown. A study by UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers sheds light on this phenomenon by showing what happens when p53 becomes disabled, revealing the gene's diverse roles in maintaining healthy metabolic activity, repressing mobile genes called retrotransposons and preventing cells from adopting features of sperm and eggs.

science.title: Nobel physics winner's pride at pioneering AI role
science.summary: Francis Halzen, winner of the Nobel Prize in physics, spoke with pride on Wednesday about his early promotion of artificial intelligence in his research on neutrinos.

science.title: Offshore wind turbine foundations may cool ocean surface by mixing seawater
science.summary: New research within the PELAgIO ECOWind project has revealed how offshore wind farms can influence ocean temperatures and mixing, and why their effects depend on local conditions.

science.title: Survey finds K-12 educators self-censor to avoid controversy over book selections
science.summary: Elementary school teachers often put such care into creating their classroom libraries: shelving multiple copies of each book, stringing lights around them to set the mood, situating beanbag chairs and magic carpet squares strategically to encourage students to settle in.

science.title: First-in-kind data set reveals insights across the world's national and regional economies
science.summary: The University of Virginia has published the Global Capitalism Index (GCI), a first-in-kind data set offering unprecedented insights into the globe's capitalism conditions in every country. Assembled from more than two hundred data sets across eight key pillars, the GCI's country-by-country scores offer an array of ways to understand capitalism around the world.

science.title: Hawaiian hot spot study uncovers evidence of true polar wander
science.summary: On Earth, everything is moving. The planet spins, the tectonic plates shift and the spin axis wobbles, as do the magnetic poles, which makes determining how things move a rather tricky proposition. For Rice University's Richard Gordon, this problem came up when he was trying to understand the history of the Hawaiian hot spot, the deep-mantle source of the volcanism that created the Hawaiian–Emperor chain of islands and underwater volcanoes.

science.title: Eight-year analysis reveals how sunlight and nutrients shape sustainable urban farming
science.summary: Factors such as sunlight and stage-specific nutrient application determine crop success in urban agriculture, far beyond fixed recipes or miracle solutions. The findings are published in the journal Agronomy for Sustainable Development.

science.title: 'Self-blinking dyes' simplify nanoscale imaging without sacrificing precision
science.summary: Nanobodies are extremely small antibody fragments that bind to specific molecules. When nanobodies are labeled with dyes, they can be used as probes to enhance super-resolution microscopy. However, conventional blinking dyes often perform poorly when attached to nanobodies, limiting their practical advantages. An international research team led by the University of Göttingen and the University Medical Center Göttingen (UMG) has now shown that self-blinking dyes—which can switch between bright and dark states on their own—bypass this limitation.

science.title: New approach to plant stress studies could yield hardier crops and medical insights
science.summary: At the University of Missouri, plant scientist Ron Mittler is rewriting the playbook for how scientists study life by asking what happens when living organisms face multiple stresses at once.

science.title: New polystyrene uses 50% plant-based material and breaks into fragments for potential recycling
science.summary: Polystyrene is used in protective packaging for televisions and electronic devices, in decorative boards and baseboards for interior construction, and in petri dishes. It is one of the world's most important plastics, with nearly 20 million tons produced each year. The material is predominantly derived from crude oil and is rarely recycled. Virgin polystyrene is often cheaper than recycled material, meaning that used products are typically incinerated or sent to landfills. Like many other plastics, polystyrene is highly resistant to degradation in the environment.

science.title: Ultrashort laser pulses let new microscope map electron interactions across thin materials
science.summary: A new type of advanced microscope (wide-field coherent multidimensional microscopy) has been developed. It uses a carefully designed sequence of ultrashort light pulses to study the behavior of high-tech materials, with potential practical applications in the study of innovative materials such as those used to build solar panels. This is the result of work by a research group of physicists from the Faculty of Sciences, Mathematics, Physics, and Natural Sciences at Università Cattolica's Brescia campus who, for the first time, have developed a "multidimensional microscope" that, in a sense, records the behavior of materials.

science.title: First global genome atlas reveals overlooked microscopic life in hundreds of lakes and reservoirs
science.summary: Tiny single-celled organisms help keep lakes clear, but some can also contaminate the water. An international research team has analyzed DNA data from 362 lakes to create the first global genome atlas of these organisms. With the findings now published in Nature Communications, the new atlas lays the foundation for faster and more precise monitoring of lakes.

science.title: Tiny plasma-grown particles enable easier magnetization reversal in materials for high-frequency electronics
science.summary: Researchers at South China University of Technology, in collaboration with the Dongguan Institute of Materials Science and Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, have developed a novel supranano multi-precipitate microstructure in amorphous soft magnetic composites using Ar/O₂ plasma treatment. By facilitating magnetic-moment reversal, this approach significantly reduced coercivity while maintaining excellent overall performance.

science.title: Acoustic experiments confirm topology can persist at gapless critical points
science.summary: Two studies on critical topology have recently been published in the journal Nature. These studies were led by the teams of Prof. Baile Zhang at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, and Prof. Jianhua Jiang at the University of Science and Technology of China, respectively. Prof. Xue-Jia Yu from the School of Physics at the Eastern Institute of Technology, Ningbo (EIT), served as a co-corresponding author on both papers and provided key theoretical guidance in the related experimental collaborations.

science.title: New display technology combines record brightness with pixels that stretch like rubber
science.summary: A research team led by Professor Jiwoong Yang of the Department of Energy Science and Engineering at DGIST has developed the world's first foundational technology for an ultrahigh-resolution stretchable quantum dot display (QLED) that can stretch freely like skin while maintaining sharp image quality. The findings were published in Nature Nanotechnology.

environment.summary: Humpback whales found in the Arabian Sea are likely a distinct subspecies, having evolved in isolation for tens of thousands of years, according to a newly published genetic analysis. “Arabian Sea humpback whales have long been an enigma to the scientific community,” lead author Rita Amaral, from the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS), said in a […]

With the other hand, she feeds it formula milk from a syringe. This is the latest rescue at the Department of National Parks and Wildlife’s rescue center […]

environment.summary: Funders of the $1.7 billion pledge to support Indigenous peoples and local communities’ land rights, announced at the 2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference, say they have exceeded the target by 35%, delivering $2.35 billion between 2021 and 2025. According to the final report of the Forest Tenure Funders Group (FTFG), in 2025 alone, donors […]

environment.title: New soil test could reveal how soil microbes help feed plants
environment.summary: Scientists have streamlined a method for measuring DNA-bound phosphorus in soil, making it cheaper and easier while preserving its accuracy. The technique could reveal how soil microbes help recycle phosphorus and ultimately support more sustainable fertilizer and nutrient management.

environment.title: 1.7-billion-year-old fossils reveal a crucial clue to the rise of complex life
environment.summary: Scientists studying ancient Australian rocks uncovered more than 12,000 fossils from some of the oldest known eukaryotes on Earth. These early complex cells lived in settings ranging from coastal mudflats to the open sea, but only where oxygen was available. Oxygen-free environments contained simpler microbes instead. The findings strengthen the idea that oxygen played a crucial role in the emergence of complex life.

environment.title: These medieval graves looked like family burials. DNA told a different story
environment.summary: Ancient DNA shows that adults and children buried together in medieval Sweden were often not members of the same immediate family, suggesting that burial choices reflected more than biological kinship. The research also revealed early gender-based burial customs and uncovered the remarkable story of a young woman who may have completed a pilgrimage across Europe.

environment.title: This new concrete is stronger and pulls CO2 from the air
environment.summary: Researchers have created a concrete mixture that is both stronger and capable of absorbing carbon dioxide. The best formula, combining zeolite with bamboo biochar, boosted compressive strength by 7.48% and tensile strength by 15% compared with conventional concrete. It also captured about 1.2 grams of CO₂ per day in laboratory testing.

environment.title: A strange circle on satellite maps turned out to be a 390-million-year-old impact crater
environment.summary: An amateur astronomer searching satellite maps for a Quebec camping spot accidentally discovered a massive ancient impact crater. Scientists later found shatter cones that confirmed the 25-kilometer-wide structure was blasted into Earth roughly 390 million years ago.

mix_items.summary: After heavy rain, Spanish cities often awaken to refreshed air and clean streets, while the rainwater itself vanishes into storm drains along with everything it swept away. Underground, however, a very different story unfolds.

mix_items.title: Snowball Earth's iron deposits may have formed through microbes living without sunlight
mix_items.summary: Iron is one of the most abundant metals on Earth's surface, yet how such massive iron ore deposits formed throughout geological history has long remained a mystery. The prevailing theory has been that ancient photosynthetic bacteria oxidized iron, causing it to precipitate and accumulate in the oceans.

mix_items.title: From jargon to impact: Teaching undergraduates the art of public communication
mix_items.summary: Articles published in The Conversation go well beyond academics writing for a general audience—they can also serve as valuable content for educators to use in the classroom.

mix_items.title: Common airway bacterium may help prepare lungs to fight pneumonia
mix_items.summary: A common bacterium found in the mouth and airways may help the lungs better defend themselves against pneumonia, according to new research from the University of Colorado Anschutz.

mix_items.title: Tiny photosynthetic organisms help transport carbon to the depths of the Baltic Sea
mix_items.summary: Tiny photosynthetic organisms in the Baltic Sea can contribute substantially to the transport of carbon from surface waters to deeper parts of the sea. A new study from the Department of Ecology, Environment and Plant Sciences at Stockholm University shows that their ability to form colonies and aggregates is an important factor determining how much of their biomass sinks.

mix_items.title: How a harmful bacterium senses iron—and why it matters for fighting infections
mix_items.summary: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a common culprit in hospital-acquired bacterial infections and is growing more resistant to antibiotics. New findings from Aaron Smith, professor of chemistry and biochemistry at UMBC, and collaborators at Oklahoma State University show how a two-protein system inside the bacterium operates like a sensitive switch: The pair detects iron both outside and inside the cell and then rewrites large parts of the microbe's metabolism in response.

mix_items.title: Protein LMOD1 offers new clues to muscle regeneration
mix_items.summary: Skeletal muscles are capable of regenerating themselves following an injury, a process that depends on muscle stem cells. In healthy resting muscle, these cells are predominantly in a quiescent state. However, following an injury, they are activated, begin to proliferate and subsequently start to develop into specialized skeletal muscle cells (differentiation). These cells then fuse with one another or with existing muscle fibers, generating new or repaired muscle fibers.

mix_items.title: Fruit fly study reveals how neural gates switch on short-term memory
mix_items.summary: A study in fruit flies led by researchers at NYU Langone Health has confirmed a long-standing suspicion about how the brain encodes short-term memories.

mix_items.title: International experience gives business leaders an edge, study finds
mix_items.summary: Business leaders with international experience play a significant role in shaping the success of their organizations and are often associated with stronger organizational performance, including higher growth, profitability and stock market performance, according to a new study published in the Journal of Management.

mix_items.title: Superbug P. aeruginosa uses two protein plugs to seal channels against antibiotics
mix_items.summary: A joint research team has identified a new mechanism underlying antibiotic resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a major multidrug-resistant "superbug." The discovery provides important clues for the development of new treatments for multidrug-resistant bacterial infections. The findings are published in the journal Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: Intranasal sufentanil-ketamine appears safe, effective for pediatric acute pain
mix_items.summary: Intranasal sufentanil-ketamine is fast-acting and appears to be well tolerated and effective at curbing acute pain for pediatric patients in the emergency department, according to a study presented at the annual European Emergency Medicine Congress, held Sept. 23–27 in Paris.

mix_items.title: Chain reaction that begins when tumor suppression gene is switched off offers clues to how cancer develops
mix_items.summary: A tumor suppressor gene known as p53 is mutated in more than half of all cancers, but how it acts to prevent cancer formation is largely unknown. A study by UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers sheds light on this phenomenon by showing what happens when p53 becomes disabled, revealing the gene's diverse roles in maintaining healthy metabolic activity, repressing mobile genes called retrotransposons and preventing cells from adopting features of sperm and eggs.

mix_items.title: Nobel physics winner's pride at pioneering AI role
mix_items.summary: Francis Halzen, winner of the Nobel Prize in physics, spoke with pride on Wednesday about his early promotion of artificial intelligence in his research on neutrinos.

mix_items.title: Children living with sickle cell can be treated safely using hydroxyurea, 10-year trial finds
mix_items.summary: New research shows the efficacy and safety of hydroxyurea treatment for sickle cell anemia at four low-income sites in Africa, with no increase in clinically diagnosed infections.

mix_items.title: HPV vaccination before pregnancy linked to lower risk of preterm birth and other major complications
mix_items.summary: Receiving the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine before pregnancy is associated with a lower risk of major pregnancy complications, including preterm birth, with a greater reduction in risk seen among women vaccinated at an earlier age, according to a large Swedish study published by The BMJ.

mix_items.title: About 13% of newly qualified nurses and midwives leave hospital work within six years
mix_items.summary: The early years of working life differ for newly qualified nurses and midwives working in hospitals and comparable graduates working in other sectors. Louise Schubert Paaske, a Ph.D. student in health economics at the Danish Centre for Health Economics (DaCHE) at the University of Southern Denmark, and her colleagues have used Danish national registers to follow the graduates' health trajectories over their first six years in employment. The study is published in the journal Communications Health.

mix_items.title: Offshore wind turbine foundations may cool ocean surface by mixing seawater
mix_items.summary: New research within the PELAgIO ECOWind project has revealed how offshore wind farms can influence ocean temperatures and mixing, and why their effects depend on local conditions.

mix_items.title: Survey finds K-12 educators self-censor to avoid controversy over book selections
mix_items.summary: Elementary school teachers often put such care into creating their classroom libraries: shelving multiple copies of each book, stringing lights around them to set the mood, situating beanbag chairs and magic carpet squares strategically to encourage students to settle in.

mix_items.title: Autonomous AI can increase clinical capacity for dermatologists
mix_items.summary: Autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) in urgent skin cancer pathways can increase clinical capacity for dermatologists, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology, held from Sept. 30 to Oct. 3 in Vienna.

mix_items.title: First-in-kind data set reveals insights across the world's national and regional economies
mix_items.summary: The University of Virginia has published the Global Capitalism Index (GCI), a first-in-kind data set offering unprecedented insights into the globe's capitalism conditions in every country. Assembled from more than two hundred data sets across eight key pillars, the GCI's country-by-country scores offer an array of ways to understand capitalism around the world.

mix_items.title: Blood flow directs signals that assign liver cells their jobs, mouse study finds
mix_items.summary: The liver is organized into distinct zones in which liver cells perform different functions. The blood vessels of the liver play an important role in this spatial organization: the endothelial cells lining the vessels provide signals that instruct neighboring liver cells and help determine their function. But how do endothelial cells know which signals to produce?

mix_items.title: Of mice and zebrafish: How scientists solved a decades-old mystery and uncovered new insights about inflammation
mix_items.summary: Sometimes you can solve a mystery with a fish but not a mouse. Sometimes you can see a biochemical process happening, but you can't study it in detail until you identify the underlying players. Sometimes separate streams of inquiry turn out to be part of the same story.

mix_items.title: Approved cancer drug may reduce kidney damage linked to nail-patella syndrome
mix_items.summary: Researchers led by Dr. Ralph Witzgall, a professor at the Chair of Molecular and Cellular Anatomy at the University of Regensburg, have deciphered a key disease mechanism underlying the hereditary kidney disorder nail-patella syndrome and identified a potential therapeutic strategy. Their findings demonstrate that an already approved drug can significantly reduce disease-causing changes. The study, which also involved researchers from the Technical University of Munich (TUM), was recently published in the journal Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: Hawaiian hot spot study uncovers evidence of true polar wander
mix_items.summary: On Earth, everything is moving. The planet spins, the tectonic plates shift and the spin axis wobbles, as do the magnetic poles, which makes determining how things move a rather tricky proposition. For Rice University's Richard Gordon, this problem came up when he was trying to understand the history of the Hawaiian hot spot, the deep-mantle source of the volcanism that created the Hawaiian–Emperor chain of islands and underwater volcanoes.

mix_items.title: Eight-year analysis reveals how sunlight and nutrients shape sustainable urban farming
mix_items.summary: Factors such as sunlight and stage-specific nutrient application determine crop success in urban agriculture, far beyond fixed recipes or miracle solutions. The findings are published in the journal Agronomy for Sustainable Development.

mix_items.title: 'Self-blinking dyes' simplify nanoscale imaging without sacrificing precision
mix_items.summary: Nanobodies are extremely small antibody fragments that bind to specific molecules. When nanobodies are labeled with dyes, they can be used as probes to enhance super-resolution microscopy. However, conventional blinking dyes often perform poorly when attached to nanobodies, limiting their practical advantages. An international research team led by the University of Göttingen and the University Medical Center Göttingen (UMG) has now shown that self-blinking dyes—which can switch between bright and dark states on their own—bypass this limitation.

mix_items.title: New approach to plant stress studies could yield hardier crops and medical insights
mix_items.summary: At the University of Missouri, plant scientist Ron Mittler is rewriting the playbook for how scientists study life by asking what happens when living organisms face multiple stresses at once.

mix_items.title: Blood marker may flag Alzheimer's-related changes in Down syndrome decades before symptoms appear
mix_items.summary: Decades before the first symptoms of Alzheimer's disease appear, some changes associated with the disease may begin to leave a trace in the blood. A study by the Sant Pau Research Institute (IR Sant Pau) has found that, in people with Down syndrome, levels of β-synuclein, a protein related to synaptic function, begin to rise in the third decade of life, long before symptoms appear and earlier than other blood biomarkers of Alzheimer's disease.

mix_items.title: New polystyrene uses 50% plant-based material and breaks into fragments for potential recycling
mix_items.summary: Polystyrene is used in protective packaging for televisions and electronic devices, in decorative boards and baseboards for interior construction, and in petri dishes. It is one of the world's most important plastics, with nearly 20 million tons produced each year. The material is predominantly derived from crude oil and is rarely recycled. Virgin polystyrene is often cheaper than recycled material, meaning that used products are typically incinerated or sent to landfills. Like many other plastics, polystyrene is highly resistant to degradation in the environment.

mix_items.title: Ultrashort laser pulses let new microscope map electron interactions across thin materials
mix_items.summary: A new type of advanced microscope (wide-field coherent multidimensional microscopy) has been developed. It uses a carefully designed sequence of ultrashort light pulses to study the behavior of high-tech materials, with potential practical applications in the study of innovative materials such as those used to build solar panels. This is the result of work by a research group of physicists from the Faculty of Sciences, Mathematics, Physics, and Natural Sciences at Università Cattolica's Brescia campus who, for the first time, have developed a "multidimensional microscope" that, in a sense, records the behavior of materials.

mix_items.title: First global genome atlas reveals overlooked microscopic life in hundreds of lakes and reservoirs
mix_items.summary: Tiny single-celled organisms help keep lakes clear, but some can also contaminate the water. An international research team has analyzed DNA data from 362 lakes to create the first global genome atlas of these organisms. With the findings now published in Nature Communications, the new atlas lays the foundation for faster and more precise monitoring of lakes.

mix_items.title: Heart recovery technique adapted for pediatric transplants
mix_items.summary: A donor heart recovery technique developed at Vanderbilt Health has been successfully adapted for children by pediatric heart transplant surgeons at Monroe Carell Jr. Children's Hospital at Vanderbilt, potentially expanding access to lifesaving heart transplants for children.

mix_items.title: Tiny plasma-grown particles enable easier magnetization reversal in materials for high-frequency electronics
mix_items.summary: Researchers at South China University of Technology, in collaboration with the Dongguan Institute of Materials Science and Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, have developed a novel supranano multi-precipitate microstructure in amorphous soft magnetic composites using Ar/O₂ plasma treatment. By facilitating magnetic-moment reversal, this approach significantly reduced coercivity while maintaining excellent overall performance.

mix_items.title: Acoustic experiments confirm topology can persist at gapless critical points
mix_items.summary: Two studies on critical topology have recently been published in the journal Nature. These studies were led by the teams of Prof. Baile Zhang at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, and Prof. Jianhua Jiang at the University of Science and Technology of China, respectively. Prof. Xue-Jia Yu from the School of Physics at the Eastern Institute of Technology, Ningbo (EIT), served as a co-corresponding author on both papers and provided key theoretical guidance in the related experimental collaborations.

mix_items.title: Flu season may be starting early; experts say get vaccinated now
mix_items.summary: Flu season may be getting a head start this year, and experts say that's a good reason not to put off your flu shot.

mix_items.title: Low-risk prostate tumors reveal molecular signs linked to more aggressive cancer
mix_items.summary: A new study revealed molecular features linked to more aggressive prostate cancer in a subset of patients who had been classified as low risk, highlighting biological differences that may not be apparent from clinical measures alone. The results could lead to new therapeutic strategies.

mix_items.title: New display technology combines record brightness with pixels that stretch like rubber
mix_items.summary: A research team led by Professor Jiwoong Yang of the Department of Energy Science and Engineering at DGIST has developed the world's first foundational technology for an ultrahigh-resolution stretchable quantum dot display (QLED) that can stretch freely like skin while maintaining sharp image quality. The findings were published in Nature Nanotechnology.

mix_items.title: First single-cell DNA analysis reveals mitochondrial damage in vulnerable Parkinson's brainstem neurons
mix_items.summary: Researchers have carried out the first single-cell analysis of mitochondrial DNA in a population of brainstem neurons that are particularly vulnerable to degeneration in Parkinson's disease.

mix_items.title: Arabian Sea humpbacks may be a unique subspecies at risk of extinction
mix_items.summary: Humpback whales found in the Arabian Sea are likely a distinct subspecies, having evolved in isolation for tens of thousands of years, according to a newly published genetic analysis. “Arabian Sea humpback whales have long been an enigma to the scientific community,” lead author Rita Amaral, from the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS), said in a […]

mix_items.title: ‘A few are afraid of the chicks’: Preparing Thailand’s rescued leopard cats for life in the wild
mix_items.summary: KHON KAEN, Thailand – A wildlife officer holds a leopard cat cub in one hand, its entire body small enough for her fingers to wrap around its torso. With the other hand, she feeds it formula milk from a syringe. This is the latest rescue at the Department of National Parks and Wildlife’s rescue center […]

mix_items.title: International pledge to fund forest rights exceeds target, but direct funding remains low
mix_items.summary: Funders of the $1.7 billion pledge to support Indigenous peoples and local communities’ land rights, announced at the 2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference, say they have exceeded the target by 35%, delivering $2.35 billion between 2021 and 2025. According to the final report of the Forest Tenure Funders Group (FTFG), in 2025 alone, donors […]

mix_items.title: New soil test could reveal how soil microbes help feed plants
mix_items.summary: Scientists have streamlined a method for measuring DNA-bound phosphorus in soil, making it cheaper and easier while preserving its accuracy. The technique could reveal how soil microbes help recycle phosphorus and ultimately support more sustainable fertilizer and nutrient management.

mix_items.title: 1.7-billion-year-old fossils reveal a crucial clue to the rise of complex life
mix_items.summary: Scientists studying ancient Australian rocks uncovered more than 12,000 fossils from some of the oldest known eukaryotes on Earth. These early complex cells lived in settings ranging from coastal mudflats to the open sea, but only where oxygen was available. Oxygen-free environments contained simpler microbes instead. The findings strengthen the idea that oxygen played a crucial role in the emergence of complex life.

mix_items.title: These medieval graves looked like family burials. DNA told a different story
mix_items.summary: Ancient DNA shows that adults and children buried together in medieval Sweden were often not members of the same immediate family, suggesting that burial choices reflected more than biological kinship. The research also revealed early gender-based burial customs and uncovered the remarkable story of a young woman who may have completed a pilgrimage across Europe.

mix_items.title: This new concrete is stronger and pulls CO2 from the air
mix_items.summary: Researchers have created a concrete mixture that is both stronger and capable of absorbing carbon dioxide. The best formula, combining zeolite with bamboo biochar, boosted compressive strength by 7.48% and tensile strength by 15% compared with conventional concrete. It also captured about 1.2 grams of CO₂ per day in laboratory testing.

mix_items.title: A strange circle on satellite maps turned out to be a 390-million-year-old impact crater
mix_items.summary: An amateur astronomer searching satellite maps for a Quebec camping spot accidentally discovered a massive ancient impact crater. Scientists later found shatter cones that confirmed the 25-kilometer-wide structure was blasted into Earth roughly 390 million years ago.

joke_ro.text: Am zis ca fac sport. Am facut: am fugit de responsabilitati.

satire_ro.title: Petrecere tristă de ziua lui Putin! N-a venit nimeni, că a dat de băut doar ceai
